claim: Morgan Stanley analyst Erik Woodring estimated Apple takes in over $25 billion annually from the Google search default deal at 95%-plus margins.
stance_target: dollar magnitude of Google TAC to Apple
scope_conditions: Morgan Stanley analyst note, Sept 3 2025 -- ANALYST ESTIMATE, not court-disclosed figure
quoted_support: Morgan Stanley's Erik Woodring estimated in a Wednesday note that Apple already takes in over $25 billion annually from Google's search deal at 95%-plus margins.

claim: Alphabet's stock rose about 8.5% and Apple's stock rose 2.8% on the day the remedies ruling was announced (Sept 2-3, 2025), reflecting the market's read that the ruling preserved the Apple-Google payment arrangement.
stance_target: market pricing treats remedy as non-disruptive / favorable to the status quo arrangement
quoted_support: Google's parent company, Alphabet, saw its stock shoot higher -- about 8.5% by 11:30 a.m. ET; Apple gained a few percent (2.8%) just for keeping its Google annuity intact.

claim: The non-exclusivity regime extends beyond legacy search to Google's AI access points -- Gemini and Assistant -- meaning Apple's prospective AI-default deals with Google are also barred from exclusivity.
stance_target: scope of the remedy vis-a-vis AI products, relevant to future Apple-Google Gemini partnership
quoted_support: Mehta's order specifically drags Google's AI access points -- Gemini, Assistant -- into the non-exclusivity regime.

claim: With exclusivity gone, Apple can run an annual auction across Safari, Spotlight, and Siri, playing Google, Microsoft, and potentially Perplexity against each other for default placement -- a structural mechanism argued to erode Google's rent over time.
stance_target: annual rebidding/non-exclusivity structurally erodes the rent (dialectic position B)
quoted_support: With exclusivity gone, Cupertino can run an annual auction across Safari, Spotlight, and Siri, playing Google, Microsoft, and maybe even Perplexity off each other like landlords deciding which cafe gets the scenic view.

claim: Critics argue the remedy is toothless: Epic's Tim Sweeney compared it to a convicted bank robber sentenced to probation who can keep robbing banks but must share data on how they do it with competitors, and DuckDuckGo's Gabriel Weinberg said the order won't force necessary changes.
stance_target: annual rebidding/non-exclusivity structurally erodes the rent -- counter-position (dialectic position A: toothless remedy)
quoted_support: Epic Games' Tim Sweeney posted on X that Google lost the liability phase but 'resoundingly' won the remedies... likening the ruling to a convicted bank robber sentenced to probation where he can 'continue robbing banks but must share data on how they rob banks with competing bank robbers.'

claim: Key implementation details -- revenue-sharing caps and compliance rules for the data-sharing and qualified-competitor provisions -- were delegated to a Technical Committee with wide discretion rather than fixed in the ruling itself, per Brave/JavaScript creator Brendan Eich's criticism.
quoted_support: Brave's Eich pointed out that the devil isn't in the decision, it's in the committees; key revenue-sharing caps and compliance rules have been punted to a technical panel with wide discretion.
